title: Uddhava Delivers Krishna's Message and the Gopis Reply
story:
For months the cowherd women of Vrindavan — the gopis — had poured their grief into the empty air after Krishna left for the city of Mathura. They had even pleaded with a honeybee once, mistaking the insect for a courier sent from him. Now at last a real messenger stood before them, a man who had truly travelled from Krishna, carrying words from his own mouth. His name was Uddhava — Krishna's friend and counsellor, a man of learning and restraint — and he had been sent for this one purpose: to bring them some word from the friend who had left them.

Before he spoke a single word of the message, Uddhava did something no one expected: he praised them. Through gifts, vows, and long self-denial, through sacrifice, study, and self-control, he told them, they had offered up sons, husbands, homes, and their own bodies to a single love — and that love had made them peerless. No one on earth had done what they had done. Only then, having honored them, did he speak Krishna's words.

The message was not an apology, and it was not a promise to return. Krishna asked them to see that he had never truly been far from them at all. Just as space and air, fire, water, and earth are found in every living thing, he said, so he was found in all things. He alone created, preserved, and ended the world, and he was pure knowing itself — free of every fault, untouched by the world's qualities. There was nothing outside him to be lost. A beloved who is far away, he said, remains close in the mind of the one who loves; so let them fix their minds wholly on him, and they would soon reach him. This, he said, was the whole heart of the scriptures, of yoga, and of the wise. And then, almost a memory spoken aloud: it was he who had played with them at night in this very forest.

The gopis did not accept it, and they did not refuse it. They answered with a grief so steady it had become its own kind of truth.

Does he remember us? they asked. Does Govinda — the lord of the cows, as they called him — who understands every shade of love, remember the nights when the moon hung bright over Vrindavan, the groves white with blossom, and he danced among us, his ankle-bells ringing, while we praised him with our songs? Will he ever come back to us, scorched by the sorrow he himself made? He has won a kingdom now and slain his enemies; why would he return to women of the forest like us? What are we, who live in the woods, to that great soul? And then the heart of it, the question behind every other question: who could bear to give up the memory of him? These rivers, these hills and forest paths, these cows, the sound of the flute — everything in this place calls back the son of Nanda, the cowherd chief who raised him, again and again. O lord, O husband of the goddess of fortune, O lord of Vrindavan, remover of sorrows.

So the exchange ended not in comfort but in a strange completion. Krishna had asked them to fix their minds on him; they answered that they could not do otherwise — that the world around them would not let them forget, and that forgetting was the one thing their love could not manage. What he had called a path to union, they had already been walking, without choosing it, from the day he left. Uddhava, who had come to teach them, stood silent, and something in the learned man began to turn.
reflection: The gopis cannot be consoled by argument because what they carry is not ignorance but love. Krishna asks for a mind fixed wholly on him, and their reply — that rivers, hills and a flute will not let them forget — is that very fixing, already accomplished. Their longing is the union he describes.
next_story_tease: But their reply undid the messenger, and Uddhava would soon wish to trade his learning for a place in the dust of their feet.
hero_scene: Uddhava standing before the gopis in a Vrindavan grove at dusk, the women gathered around him, their faces lifted as they answer that every river, hill and the sound of the flute will not let them forget Krishna.
